tip_title: Your Home Policy Might Pay You Less Than You Expect After a Claim
topic: Replacement Cost vs. Actual Cash Value Home Insurance
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Your Home Policy Might Pay You Less Than You Expect After a Claim**

Most homeowners assume a claim pays out what it costs to replace the damaged stuff. Not always. There are two ways your policy can value a loss: replacement cost coverage pays to replace or repair with a new equivalent, no depreciation taken out. Actual cash value coverage subtracts depreciation first, so a five-year-old roof or a three-year-old TV gets paid out at today's worn-down value, not at what it costs to replace it. The difference on a significant claim can be thousands of dollars, and a lot of people don't realize which version they have until after the loss.

Not sure how your policy handles it? Your Peachy agent can pull up your declarations page and tell you exactly what you've got in about ten minutes.

📖 [Learn more from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners](https://content.naic.org/article/whats-difference-between-actual-cash-value-coverage-and-replacement-cost-coverage)
summary: Explains the functional difference between replacement cost value and actual cash value coverage in homeowners policies, focused on how depreciation affects a claim payout and why it matters at claim time.
scoring_notes: Both audiences are majority homeowners (East Cobb 78%). No prior coverage of this subject in the last 6 months. Highly actionable — readers can check their declarations page today. Timeliness boosted by July storm season in Georgia, when actual claims are more top-of-mind. Strong crossover tip for both audiences. Trusted source (naic.org). No carrier names, no dollar figures for premiums.

tip_title: Your Teen Is Behind the Wheel This Summer. Here's How to Manage the Insurance Hit.
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Your Teen Is Behind the Wheel This Summer. Here's How to Manage the Insurance Hit.**

Adding a teen driver to your auto policy is one of the bigger premium jumps a family can face, and summer is when those young drivers are logging the most miles. What a lot of parents don't realize is that there are legitimate discount levers you can pull right now. A good student discount, available to teens who maintain at least a B average, is one of the most common and most underused. Completing a recognized driver education or defensive driving course is another one that many carriers reward with a reduced rate. These aren't tiny tweaks, they can meaningfully offset the cost of having a new driver on your policy. Fall semester is coming up fast, and that's when the good student discount resets, so it's worth getting this on your radar before school starts.

Not sure which discounts your teen qualifies for or whether they're properly listed on your policy? Your Peachy agent can walk through it with you.

📖 [Learn more from the Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/auto-insurance-teen-drivers)
summary: Covers how adding a teen driver affects auto insurance premiums and the specific discount levers (good student discount, driver ed/defensive driving courses) that can reduce the cost, framed as a summer/back-to-school action item.
scoring_notes: All three audiences have meaningful teen-driver household populations. East Cobb explicitly flagged as teen/college-age kids. Lewisville Lake is family-heavy. July is peak teen driving season and the fall semester discount reset creates a concrete near-term action. No overlap with prior covered topics. iii.org is a trusted source. Good student and driver ed discount angles are specific and actionable, not vague. Category is auto, diversified from recent home-heavy tips.
